title: Working With Defilements and Hinderances
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton shares a personal journey of applying Buddhist teachings to navigate the challenges of politics and activism, finding balance and clarity through a three-step process: observing one's mind, acknowledging emotions, and rationalizing actions. By cultivating mindfulness and awareness, they've learned to recognize their own limitations, work with negative emotions, and focus on personal growth rather than trying to change others. This practice has allowed them to stay focused, avoid burnout, and make more informed decisions, ultimately leading to a greater sense of calmness and clarity in their efforts to create positive change.

sentences.text: Good evening.
Happy New Year, we hope.
I have to take off my glasses in order to read.
This evening I want to talk about some classical Buddhist teachings on the defilements and the hindrances.
Therefore I have my chart.
Greed, hate, delusion are the defilements, sometimes called other things.
Hindrances are sometimes called these: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and worry, and doubt.
I'm going to talk about these, but I'm going to get at them through a back door.
Our current civic and political situation provides us with the perfect opportunity to practice with the defilements and the hindrances.
But don't tense up, I'm not going to rant about politics.
I want to share with you how these teachings are helping me to work with what's going on in the world this past year.
My hope is that hearing what I've been doing will stimulate you to think of some things that you could be doing with those problems or other kinds of problems.
We Buddhists take the Bodhisattva vow to save all beings.
This vow reminds us that we are all interconnected and that what each of us does affects everyone.
Could someone turn the lights up a bit, because I'm having a little trouble seeing my script here?
Thank you.
The Bodhisattva vow inspires us to keep trying to do even what seems impossible, because we are all interconnected.
After the 2016 presidential election, I made a similar personal vow to help save our democracy by being active politically through to the 2018 election.
That's two years of activity.
Knowing I couldn't do this alone, my first action was to find other people to join.
And I did find two or three groups.
One was the climate change lobby, which has a local chapter, which educates citizens and members of Congress about climate change and what we can do about it to reduce it.

The second was the political action group Indivisible, that maybe some of you know about, which is educating people to contact their members of Congress and give them information about what we think should be done.
Make regular phone calls to them.
And it also seems like I took another group, too, but maybe that was it.
I took a bunch of online courses as well.

First was lobbying training with the Friends Committee on National Legislation, which has a good online course on how to lobby politely, being courteous to people when you call them, but still stating what you want to say.
Climate change [unclear: "chain"] training was also through a national organization, and Ecosattva training on climate change from the Buddhist perspective.
There's lots of good information I found online, and a lot of it is free, so anyone could get that.
So these steps prepared me to act.

Acting means becoming informed, which means learning about really unpleasant, alarming things, such as the cancellation of EPA programs and climate research, dozens of professional State Department jobs unfilled, lack of legislation on gun violence despite continued mass killings, not to speak of the daily fire hose of misinformation and tweets.
The onslaught is very upsetting.
And I had this goal of being active every day, doing something, communicating something, learning something new, trying to do something about it.
And I didn't like this onslaught.
It was very unpleasant.
I would rather have turned away.
But if I was to live up to my vow, I had to pay attention.
In fact, this is what Buddhism calls us to do: face what's happening.
So I took that seriously.
So I began working with my mind.
I soon realized that I was dealing with the second noble truth.
What our experience is, is how we react to events, to what's happening.
Our experience: desire or aversion or ignorance.
These are things that we bring to the actual situation.
These defilements wreck our equanimity, our peace of mind, our groundedness.
As the daily news onslaught hit me, I began to observe my mind.
I noticed anger, alarm, desire to hit back.
These harsh feelings diverted me from my goal of trying to influence my members of Congress politely, courteously.
How could I call them if I was wanting to yell at them?
I had to get past these feelings.
Knowing that we must acknowledge feelings before we can release them or get past them, I started to look at them and accept them.
I gave them space to be what they were in me.
I didn't add my thoughts to why I felt those things or why I was justified in feeling them.
I just stayed with them for a few minutes, maybe only a couple of minutes.
And when I did this, they subsided, just like we've been taught.
They fell away almost immediately.
As long as I said, "Oh, you're there," my equilibrium recovered.
In such an instance, once I felt more balanced, I could remember my vow to do something about this.
In the midst of feeling these strong feelings, I couldn't remember.
But if I paid attention and they kind of said, "Oh, okay," and were quiet, then I could think again and decide what to do.
Do something appropriate.
Call a member of Congress and talk to a staff person.
Or call somebody in the state or somebody in the federal government.
Email instead.
Or talk to somebody, a sympathetic friend, if I was having trouble figuring out what to do next.
Almost always there was an emotional reactivity, and then it subsided if I paid attention to it.
And then I could figure out an action.
Maybe not immediately, but within a few hours, or the next day, worst case.
By not getting caught up in my initial emotional reaction, I can do what the Buddha taught: not cling or push away.
Which clears the way to decide rationally what to do, or to realize I don't know what to do, but I will figure out something over time.
So I discovered, and now use daily, the following three steps.
One, perceive what's going on.
Two, fully feel and acknowledge my reactions and feelings.
And once I've calmed down, because I always calm down as soon as I acknowledge them, then I can rationally figure out what to do.
I have noticed that it's easy to get caught in step two.
It's easy to wallow a bit.
Feeling my strong reaction easily leads to feeling helpless if I stay too long with it.
Or if I resist doing it, then I feel helpless longer.
So I really have to address the feeling.
Acknowledge it and accept it.
Knowing that my bad feelings will subside is a good motivator to look at them, because they will go away if I just give them space.
And then I can move on to being rational.
Early on in my efforts this past year to learn how to do this and to influence my members of Congress, a challenge arose for me around calling them.
I've always been phone phobic.
I hate cold calling.
When I was in business for myself, it took me every week until Thursday to get up the nerve to call anybody.
So it was really bad.
Sometimes it's still Thursday before I do this.
I'm afraid I'll get my words mixed up or I'll make a fool of myself.
Or worse, I won't make my point effectively.
In the training I took through the Friends Committee, the goal is always to be respectful and rational in these calls.
Never to be angry.
Never to yell at anybody.
To achieve this and prepare to make an effective call, I do the following things.
If the issue is one best addressed in a phone call, it is time sensitive.
You've got to get it before the bill goes to the floor.
I write out what I want to say.
I sometimes use scripts that are provided for me by different organizations, and I try to say what they recommend.
I practice what I'm going to say aloud.
I find that if I hear my voice, I know where I'm scared or where I'm uncertain, where I don't have the right information, where I can't pronounce the words properly.
And so it's really a good test.
And I have to practice several times aloud sometimes.
After several attempts, if I can't get myself to phone, I still feel afraid, I give in and allow myself to email, because that's easier for me to do.
So what to do when I can't get myself to do either email or phone calling?
This is a time for me to observe my mind more.
I usually find that I'm afraid for various reasons.
I don't understand the issue well enough to talk about it, either in writing or on the phone.
So I need to learn more.
Sometimes I don't have enough time to learn about the thing before it's urgent to call.
That puts me in a real bind.
My fear of being a fool, of wanting to be perfect, is obstructing me just in general.
Or the issue is very complex, as many of them are, and I don't know enough about it to be able to talk reasonably or write reasonably about it.
I just don't know.
Realizing where I am in this spectrum is calming and helps me settle down.
I need to back off for a while, take a break, put the issue on a back burner, let it simmer back there in my unconscious.
And when I do this, it percolates.
And eventually, in a day or two, I think of something to do and I do it.
And I'm able to do it pretty quickly.
I make a real effort not to let it drift away.
I make a commitment to do something about this thing that I'm concerned about.
And I track all of my...
This will tell you how compulsive I am.
I track all of my phone calls and emails.
C for call and E for email.
This notebook is not totally full with these, but it's got lots of pages.
And this is a motivator for me to do it, because I can write it down and say, yay, check, that kind of thing.
So that helps me do it.
Also, it's a good record, because many of the issues are pretty similar to each other, and so I don't know who I've written to unless I have a record of it.
So that's my trick to trick myself.
Occasionally, when I find I'm repeatedly resisting doing action, now here again I'm working with my mind here and all this stuff.
This is mind stuff.
I realize that I'm feeling overwhelmed, and there's nothing I can do at that point.
Too many issues, too little information, too much emotion and confusion.
So I've learned to give myself an occasional break, a time out.
I need a different story for a while.
So I read a good novel.
That's somebody else's story.
Or I go to a good movie, somebody else's story.
Or I go to the Y and talk to people, strangers to me who are working out, just so I get a sense of community.
And last year I told Bernadette that one of the things I was going to try to do was talk to people I didn't know.
And she bought me this crazy cup.
I have all these really goofy-looking people on the front.
And it says, as you start to drink it, "Talk to strangers."
It's wonderful.
So that's been my model.
And I'm having a good time doing that, to try to get a sense for myself that I'm not alone, but also to give everyone that I meet recognition that they're not alone either.
This past year I found that I also got overwhelmed from trying to respond to too many issues.
There's hundreds of them and they're coming across in the computer, dozens and dozens every day.

So over time I managed to identify a few issues that are most important to me: climate change, gun control, health care, and issues of democracy like voters' rights and ethics in the government and so forth.
Many, many more issues pull at me.
And I don't get rid of certain, probably ten or twelve or fifteen, email sources that come to me daily that I don't respond to, but I don't want to not know about them.
So there's always a kind of transaction I have to do with myself, as I know you're there, but I can't do everything.
So I try to limit my activity and my responsiveness to things that I can actually do, otherwise I'll just burn out.
And my goal is to help, so I have to work within my capacity.
So my political concerns actually have turned out to motivate me to work with my mind following Buddhist teachings.
This actually has been always my way of practicing Buddhism: to look at what's happening in my life, how do I respond to it, how do the teachings help me to do that.
So I've always been somebody living in the world where there are many challenges.
Our cultural and political turmoil has been perfect for practicing with the defilements and the five hindrances.
I'll say a little bit more about them now.
The defilements, greed, hate, and delusion, impede us from right understanding, right thinking, right acting, right speaking, greed, hatred, delusion.
Every day I pay attention to what's happening in the world, and I encounter one or all three of these in my mind, and I try to recognize that I'm experiencing them.
This releases them.
Working with the defilements starts with mindfulness.
There is a little book about mindfulness and the defilements by Ashen Tejanecha, Tejanea, who was a Burmese, who is, perhaps he's still alive, a Vipassana teacher in Myanmar.
He wrote a treatise on working with the defilements, and it's been made into this little book called *Don't Look Down on the Defilements.
They Will Laugh at You.* I want to read various sentences that are pertinent to what I'm talking about.
This is not a whole paragraph or anything, but a selection.
*Meditation is mind work, the work of being aware.
When you pay attention to your body, you will notice many sensations.
The more relaxed you are, the easier it is to develop mindfulness.
So you must know whether you are feeling tense or relaxed.
We all have wrong attitudes.
We cannot help having them.
So do not try to have the right attitude.
Try to recognize if you have the wrong or the right attitude instead.
It's important to be aware when you have right attitudes, but it is even more important to recognize and investigate your wrong attitudes.
Try to understand your wrong attitudes.
Find out how they affect your practice and see how they make you feel.
So watch yourself and keep checking to see what state of mind you are practicing with.
Do not reject what is happening.
Rejecting what is happening is aversion.
Not knowing that something is happening or has stopped happening is delusion.
You are not trying to make things turn out the way you want them to happen.
You are trying to know what is happening as it is.
Thinking things should be this way or that, wanting this or that to happen or not to happen is expectation.
Expectations create anxiety and can lead to aversion.
It is important that you become aware of your attitudes.*
Such kind teachings.
*Get to know the defilements that arise in your mind.
As you stop attaching to or identifying with the defilements, their strength will slowly diminish.
You will simply want to see things as they are.*
A second helpful teaching is about the five hindrances and how they prevent us from having insight and feeling free in our minds.
Sensual desire, the first, for pleasant rather than unpleasant things, restricts us.
Ill will, which is hostility, anger, resentment, separates us from each other.
Sloth and torpor, like weariness, exhaustion, burnout, depression, limits us.
Restlessness and worry, such as anxiety, scattered mind, fear, distracts us.
Doubt, lack of confidence, suspicion of others discourages and depresses us.
I experience each of these, and it's helpful to become aware that I am feeling and thinking them.
Awareness or mindfulness diminishes their power.
It releases me to think rationally and to get back to work.
Gil Fronsdale has written a lovely book recently called *Unhindered*, about the hindrances.
Actually Marty gave me this book, and she also told me about this other one that I just read from.
Sorry, thank you Marty for these gifts to help me through my political ruminations this year.
Let me read a little bit from what Gil says about ill will.
*The first of the five hindrances are sensual desire and ill will.
These two hindrances are directly connected to how and where our attention is directed.
Often it is directed at the object of our desire or ill will.*
You can't say that.
That kind of thing.
*Mindfulness practice is dependent on our ability to choose what we give attention.
Rather than allowing strong desire and ill will to continue unchecked, when we practice mindfulness we choose to direct attention to examine these hindrances.
Through sufficient investigation, understanding and non-reactivity, they can lose their power to preoccupy our attention.
With enough insight we can even become free of them.*
The book has a whole system for looking at all of the hindrances and reflecting on them, and has questions and so forth.
I'm thinking maybe to have a little class in the fall about that that we could all do together.
I think it might be a way of helping each other to think about those things.
I think maybe there's another page.
That was it.
So in sum, it turns out very ironically that a political situation has created an opportunity for me to learn about these things and to study my mind in greater detail actually than before.
It's a perfect opportunity as a matter of fact for me because I'm interested in politics.
I don't mean to proselytize you and say you've got to get politically active, but all of us have in our lives challenges at work or with other people or with our families.
Always there's something that we can focus on and practice with these concepts and these teachings.
Being mindful is grounding and calming.
That's what the Buddha taught.
And the truth is we can't change anybody else.
We can only change ourselves.
But when we do change for the better, everyone benefits because we're all interconnected.
Thank you.
There's a few moments for questions or rebuttals.
**Participant:** Another hindrance, it just mentions sensual desire.
Where do you place the desire for change?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Mental.
Yeah, mental.
I think that's one of them.
So where would you put that?
You could think of the mind as a sense.
I think it has been in Buddhist teachings.
What I want, what I want.
If nobody wants to say anything.
**Participant:** In the whittling down process, how do you go about making those decisions?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** The whittling down, oh, there's just too much, I can't address everything.
It's because of repetition.
Because what I respond to, what I feel most passionately about happens more strongly so I can notice it better.
But also I am concerned and I read up more on those things so I know that I'm aware of it.
So I decided that I could just limit myself.
It came about rather naturally, but it took maybe almost as much as half the year, the past year, to recognize where my real serious concerns were.
I'm concerned about a lot of things.
But I can't invest in more than about four of them with any success, and respond and so forth.
And sometimes not very much there because those keep changing and new information comes up.
I couldn't hold down a job and do this at the same time.
Does that answer what you were asking?
**Participant:** I applaud your bravery going into this form.
Are there certain things that you had to put aside to be able to focus?
Like not getting away from the news on a daily basis?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Well, I did sort of say to myself I'm going to pay attention, so I couldn't leave the news out.
I really needed to get that.
But I do turn off certain situations that are discouraging to me.
You don't need to hear the same thing six times.
**Participant:** Yeah, right, right.
What tends to happen?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** But I have limited some of my other activities.
Because this is a major activity, I have made this a priority.
So I don't do some of the things that maybe I was inclined to do before.
**Participant:** Since you've committed yourself to this process, do you find you can even listen to the news a little bit with a better heart?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I listen critically maybe.
I read the Times in the morning and I'm looking for information for the things that I'm most interested in.
So it's a project, it has some kind of structure to it.
**Participant:** To help your commitment.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yeah, yeah.
Thank you very much.
**Participant:** You touched on this, but I wonder if you could...
I realize this is probably related to the category of doubt.

I find when I use the information that comes, there's one thing after another and it touches on so many different areas, and is infused with, just say, lies, that I feel very overwhelmed at knowing how to function, because the truth and right action doesn't seem to have impact in the face of that.
So I wonder if those hindrances, if those feelings have come up for you in your experiences in working with them.
It feels a little bit different to me than say how I react when anger comes up about what's happening.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Well, I'm very discouraged by apparent lies, and repeatedly.
I think it's very depressing and I do feel helpless.
But I've noticed that I'm getting tougher, intellectually tougher about that kind of thing.
And I can recognize that I'm saying, I don't think that's probably...
It may not be quite a lie.
That may be a perspective, a different perspective.
Or if something that I agree with is stated extra strongly, I'm a little suspicious that it's exaggerated.
So I'm getting a little more discerning through the process of listening to and being aware of things with this object in mind of the goal.
The goal has really helped me to not be overcome by this stuff.
What's really being said here?
How do I actually really see this?
And that allows, I think, one to be more even in terms of how to perceive.
**Participant:** So you don't get caught up in the emotional judgment of it.
Is that part of what you're saying?
**Shuko Edie Norton:** And I won't name names, but there are certain voices, tones of voice, that I just turn off because they're so discouraging to me.
So I don't listen.
Click, clicker, or radio click.
Power.
But that helps me to not have to submit myself to that.
**Participant:** I really applaud you for your effort.
I really honor that.
Thank you for doing it.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Well, you're welcome.
And you can come too.
**Participant:** I cannot be politically active.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** We're all active in some arena.
We all have to help, and we are helping.
**Participant:** I'm really in awe how you're tackling this and your persistence and your doing it.
That's just awesome.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Thank you.
Thank you.
**Participant:** I notice that when I read, I get the New York Times, and I read the Times, and I can be a lot more objective, and more engaged and more reactive, I've become.
But I've noticed, when I listen, I hear this commentary going on in my head, when I'm saying whatever comes to my mind.
But I've been implying, sometimes I just listen to just see how reactive I'm going to be and what comes up.
And as I get more mindful about it, my reactions haven't been over the top anyway.
They're really reducing in that way.
So some days I know all I can do is read, and that'll be fine.
And then other days I feel like I can handle listening to something today.
And that's just kind of how I've been.
I've been taking the cue from these teachings about relaxing.
Because if you're tense, I mean, anger or dismay makes you tense.
And in order to feel that feeling and to allow it to be there, you do kind of have to relax and breathe a bit.
So the relaxing actually helps a great deal to release the tension.
So it's an interesting dynamic that I hadn't actually applied.
I was always in my head trying to understand and articulate something.
Now I'm just in my body receiving.
And then I later think and later articulate it.
It's taken me the whole year though to get to the point where I don't really do that.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yeah, me too.
Only a year.
**Participant:** Well, I have a moment though.
When I do this today, it depends on which party the information is coming from.
And I really have been watching, oh, I have a different reaction to the same action, or whatever is coming across.
They were talking about today the North Carolina thing, redistricting in North Carolina.
And they were talking about, okay, this is a Republican thing, right, North Carolina state.
And I went, hi, whatever.
And then they were saying, [unclear: "Ann"], the Democrats have done it in, I forget what state.
And no, I just don't have this kind of reaction.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yeah, interesting.
**Participant:** So that really helps me to see that, to see the contrast and just to recognize myself.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Our frame, yeah.
You don't have to feel this.
Time, thank you very much, everyone.
Place with the truth.
